case_brief.incident_description: Thabo worked for the employer for five years. He was accused of insubordination after refusing to drive a delivery vehicle that he said had faulty brakes. He asked for the instruction to be put in writing. He was told at 08:00 that a disciplinary hearing would take place at 10:00 the same day. He was not allowed to bring a colleague. His direct manager, who had issued the instruction, chaired the hearing. Thabo denied being insubordinate and said he was concerned about safety. He was dismissed immediately after the hearing.
case_brief.original_client_narrative: I refused to drive the truck because the brakes were faulty. My manager said I was insubordinate and then chaired my hearing two hours later. I was not allowed anyone with me and I was fired the same day.
legal_basis: Occupational Health and Safety Act context
case_brief.recommended_next_step: Without Prejudice settlement letter addressing procedural unfairness and the safety context.
weaknesses: Employer may argue refusal of instruction was misconduct

letter:
Background

1. We act on the instructions of our client, Mr Thabo Mokoena, in connection with the termination of his employment with Northstar Logistics (Pty) Ltd on 21 October 2026. This letter is written without prejudice and subject to contract. Nothing in this letter constitutes an admission of fact or liability on our client's part, and all of our client's rights are reserved to pursue the appropriate legal remedies, including referral to the Commission for Conciliation, Mediation and Arbitration, without further notice should this matter not be resolved.

2. Our client reports that he was employed by Northstar Logistics (Pty) Ltd for a period of five years to the date of his dismissal. To the extent that this period reflects continuous and uninterrupted service, we record this on the basis of our client's account, pending confirmation from your records.

3. On 21 October 2026, our client was instructed to drive a delivery vehicle which he says he believed, on reasonable grounds, had faulty brakes. He raised this safety concern and asked that the instruction be confirmed in writing before he complied. Our client was then informed, at approximately 08:00 that same morning, that a disciplinary hearing concerning the allegation would be convened at 10:00 the same day. This afforded our client in the region of two hours' notice of a hearing with potentially serious consequences for his employment.

4. Our client was not permitted to bring a colleague or union representative to the hearing. It is material to record that the hearing was chaired by his direct manager, who had issued the original instruction to drive the vehicle. The allegation of insubordination arose from our client's refusal to comply with that instruction, and the manager's own conduct in issuing it was therefore directly implicated in the matter under consideration. At the hearing, our client denied that his conduct amounted to insubordination and maintained that his refusal was motivated by a genuine concern for his own safety and the safety of other road users. He was dismissed immediately upon the conclusion of the hearing, the same day.

Legal Claims

1. Unfair dismissal: substantive and procedural fairness under section 188 of the LRA: Section 188(1) of the Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995 provides that a dismissal is unfair unless the employer shows that the reason for dismissal is a fair reason related to the employee's conduct or capacity, or based on the employer's operational requirements, and that the dismissal was effected in accordance with a fair procedure. The applicable framework for assessing both elements is found in the Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025, which replaced the former Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025, in particular paragraphs 7 to 10 on fair reason, sanction and consistency, and paragraph 11 on fair procedure. On the substantive question, our client disputes that his conduct constituted insubordination at all. He refused the instruction in circumstances where he says he held a genuine and reasonably held belief that the vehicle presented a safety risk, and he sought written confirmation of the instruction rather than an outright refusal to work. Where an employee's reluctance to comply with an instruction arises from a bona fide safety concern, this is a material factor going to whether the conduct was a dismissible offence at all, and whether dismissal was a proportionate response in the context of five years of service and, on our client's account, no prior disciplinary record. On the procedural question, the defects are significant. Our client was given approximately two hours' notice of a hearing that resulted in the termination of five years' employment, which does not afford a reasonable opportunity to prepare a response or secure representation, contrary to paragraph 11 of the Code. He was denied the right to be accompanied by a fellow employee or union representative, a core element of a fair hearing under the Code. The hearing was also chaired by the same manager who issued the instruction said to have been disobeyed, meaning the person adjudicating the allegation had a direct personal connection to its outcome and could not readily be seen to bring an independent mind to the proceedings. Taken together, these procedural features are substantial and, independently of the substantive dispute, expose the dismissal to a real risk of a finding of procedural unfairness.

Without Prejudice Settlement Proposal

Without conceding any claim and while our client's rights remain fully reserved, our client is amenable to resolving this matter on a without prejudice and commercially sensible basis, in order to avoid the time and cost associated with CCMA proceedings for both parties. Our client proposes the following terms of settlement:

• Compensation on an ex gratia, total cost to company basis. In light of the cumulative procedural defects identified above, together with the disputed substantive basis for dismissal and the safety context giving rise to the allegation, our client's position is that settlement should be calibrated toward the higher end of the compensation range available under section 194(1) of the LRA, being up to twelve months' remuneration

• Payment of an ex gratia settlement amount on a total cost to company basis, calibrated toward the higher end of the compensation range available under section 194(1) of the LRA, being up to twelve months' remuneration. This calibration reflects, specifically: the absence of reasonable notice of the hearing, our client having been given approximately two hours to prepare in respect of a hearing that determined five years of employment; the denial of his right to be accompanied by a fellow employee or union representative; the fact that the hearing was chaired by the same manager who issued the underlying instruction, raising a direct question as to the independence of the decision-maker; and the substantive dispute as to whether a refusal founded on a bona fide safety concern was properly characterised as insubordination at all. Each of these factors independently increases the litigation risk this matter presents at the CCMA, and cumulatively they support settlement calibration at the higher end of the available range

• Payment in lieu of notice calculated by reference to the applicable notice period under section 37 of the BCEA, subject to any more favourable contractual notice entitlement, with payment made in accordance with section 38 of the BCEA

• Payment of any accrued but untaken leave pay owing to our client under section 40 of the BCEA

• Written confirmation that any pension or provident fund contributions due on our client's behalf have been paid up to date, and that the accumulated benefit will be dealt with in accordance with the rules of the applicable fund

• Written confirmation that UIF contributions have been paid up to date, together with a completed UI-19 certificate to enable our client to access unemployment benefits

• Issue of a certificate of service in terms of section 42 of the BCEA

• Provision of an agreed reference, in terms to be agreed between the parties. This is proposed as a standard-form term and remains subject to our client's confirmation of instruction as to its precise content

• An undertaking by Northstar Logistics (Pty) Ltd and its representatives not to disparage our client to any third party, including prospective employers

• An undertaking of confidentiality as to the terms of settlement, the negotiations and the existence of this dispute, as between the parties and their respective advisers

• Confirmation that the disciplinary finding and any related record of the allegation of insubordination will be expunged from our client's personnel file. This term is proposed as a standard-form settlement provision and remains subject to confirmation of instruction

• The terms set out above to be recorded in a formal written settlement agreement, to be prepared and signed by both parties, with all of our client's rights reserved until such time as that agreement is concluded

Our client holds relevant evidence going to each of the matters set out above, including the timeline of events on 21 October 2026, and is in a position to pursue a referral to the CCMA within the applicable 30-day period under section 191(1)(b)(i) of the LRA should this matter not be resolved. We invite a substantive response to this letter within seven calendar days of receipt, failing which our client will proceed to refer this dispute for conciliation and, if necessary, arbitration without further notice.

All of our client's rights are expressly reserved.

criteria.problem: The draft states as fact that the manager 'had issued the original instruction' and that this manager's 'own conduct in issuing it was therefore directly implicated in the matter under consideration', and later frames the hearing chair as having a 'direct personal connection to its outcome'. This is consistent with the brief (proc_chair: false, manager chaired and issued instruction) so is supported. However, the draft's characterisation that the manager's involvement in chairing somehow means he 'laid' or initiated the charge goes slightly beyond the brief, which only confirms he chaired the hearing and issued the original work instruction, not that he brought the disciplinary charge. The brief does not confirm who formally brought or laid the charge. The draft does not explicitly say the manager laid the charge, but the phrase 'the manager's own conduct in issuing it was therefore directly implicated in the matter under consideration' blurs this line and risks being read as alleging the manager both instigated and adjudicated the charge, which is not expressly confirmed.
criteria.required_fix: Soften the phrase to describe the manager's dual role (instruction-giver and hearing chair) descriptively without implying he personally brought or laid the charge, since that fact is not confirmed in the brief.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: 'the hearing was chaired by his direct manager, who had issued the original instruction to drive the vehicle... the manager's own conduct in issuing it was therefore directly implicated in the matter under consideration.'

criteria.problem: The draft fails the mandatory current-law check: the Code citation is inconsistent and self-contradictory. It cites 'Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025' correctly on first use within the legal claim, but then states this 'replaced the former Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025', which is an internal contradiction (it cannot replace an instrument with the identical name) and risks confusing the current 2025 Code with the repealed Schedule 8 instrument without naming it. Additionally, the section 188(1) anchor is present before the Code discussion, which is correct. The settlement compensation narrative does connect value to procedural/substantive risk in reasonable depth, satisfying the HIGH-merit specificity requirement. However, the Code citation defect is a mandatory current-law failure.
criteria.required_fix: Correct the citation so it reads cleanly, for example: 'The applicable framework ... is found in the Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025, in particular paragraphs 7 to 10 on fair reason, sanction and consistency, and paragraph 11 on fair procedure.' Remove the erroneous self-referential 'replaced the former' clause entirely, or if intending to reference the repealed Schedule 8 instrument, this must not be named or implied at all per the current-law override.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: 'The applicable framework for assessing both elements is found in the Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025, which replaced the former Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025, in particular paragraphs 7 to 10...'

criteria.problem: Tone is largely professional, controlled and proportionate, consistent with counterparty-facing house style, using restrained formulations such as 'It is material to record' and 'our client's position is'. No bluster or stock aggressive phrasing. Minor concern: the phrase 'could not readily be seen to bring an independent mind to the proceedings' is slightly argumentative/editorialising in a way that borders on asserting a conclusion of bias rather than identifying a procedural risk factor, though it remains within acceptable bounds for a WP letter.
criteria.required_fix: Consider softening to 'raises a material question as to the independence of the decision-maker' (already used later) to avoid duplicative and slightly overreaching framing in two places.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: 'the person adjudicating the allegation had a direct personal connection to its outcome and could not readily be seen to bring an independent mind to the proceedings.'

criteria.problem: There is significant content duplication between the first settlement term and the second settlement term: both describe the ex gratia compensation calibrated to 'the higher end of the compensation range... up to twelve months' remuneration', with the second repeating almost verbatim and then adding the risk-factor narrative. This creates a redundant, bloated settlement clause structure rather than a single clean compensation clause, contrary to the house style expectation that settlement clauses be in the standing order without duplicated content.
criteria.required_fix: Merge the two settlement terms into a single compensation clause that states the ex gratia compensation proposal once and then sets out the risk factors supporting that calibration, removing the duplicate opening sentence.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: Term 1: 'Compensation on an ex gratia, total cost to company basis... calibrated toward the higher end of the compensation range available under section 194(1)...' Term 2: 'Payment of an ex gratia settlement amount on a total cost to company basis, calibrated toward the higher end of the compensation range available under section 194(1)... being up to twelve months' remuneration. This calibration reflects, specifically...'

criteria.problem: Mandatory current-law check failure: the notice-pay clause treats BCEA section 37 and section 38 ambiguously. It states 'Payment in lieu of notice calculated by reference to the applicable notice period under section 37 of the BCEA, subject to any more favourable contractual notice entitlement, with payment made in accordance with section 38 of the BCEA.' While this does reference both sections, it does not make clear that section 37 sets the period and section 38 is the complementary payment mechanism that applies specifically because notice was not worked; it is serviceable but slightly underexplains the complementary relationship, falling short of making the two sections unambiguously complementary as required. This is a borderline defect bordering on acceptable, but given the mandatory check is strict, it is flagged as insufficiently explicit.
criteria.required_fix: Revise to explicitly state the complementary relationship, e.g. 'Payment in lieu of the notice period to which our client is entitled under section 37 of the BCEA (or any more favourable contractual notice period), such payment to be made in accordance with section 38 of the BCEA as payment in lieu of notice not worked.' The response window of seven calendar days is correctly stated and compliant.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: 'Payment in lieu of notice calculated by reference to the applicable notice period under section 37 of the BCEA, subject to any more favourable contractual notice entitlement, with payment made in accordance with section 38 of the BCEA'

criteria.problem: Two mandatory defects found: (1) the self-contradictory Code of Practice citation risking confusion with the repealed Schedule 8 instrument ('Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025, which replaced the former Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025'); (2) no case-law citations and no rand figures are present, which is compliant; (3) no duplicate salutation/closing/signature since those are template-supplied and correctly excluded from Part A; (4) the non-disparagement clause is correctly one-way against the employer only, compliant with the brief. The primary compliance failure is the Code citation self-contradiction, which is a mandatory current-law check failure and independently triggers the quality floor.
criteria.required_fix: Remove the internally contradictory 'which replaced the former Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025' clause and cite the 2025 Code cleanly and singly, with no reference, direct or implied, to Schedule 8 or any repealed instrument.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: 'the Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025, which replaced the former Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025, in particular paragraphs 7 to 10'

what_is_strong: The factual background paragraph on the short notice, denial of representation and the manager-as-chair conflict is well particularised with specific times (08:00, 10:00) and ties each procedural defect precisely to the Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025 paragraph 11 requirements.

The safety-related substantive defence is handled with appropriate conditional language ('he says he believed, on reasonable grounds') rather than asserting it as established fact, which respects the evidentiary discipline required for a WP letter.

The settlement terms largely follow the standing 3A.10 order (compensation, notice, leave, pension/provident, UIF, certificate of service, reference, non-disparagement, confidentiality, expungement, agreement to follow) and the response window of seven calendar days is correctly stated and within the permitted maximum.
No case-law citations and no rand figures appear anywhere in the draft, which is compliant with the house style prohibition.
what_needs_work: The Code of Practice citation is self-contradictory ('Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025, which replaced the former Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025') and must be corrected to a single clean citation with no implied reference to the repealed Schedule 8 instrument. This is a mandatory current-law failure that alone triggers the quality floor.
The two compensation-related settlement terms are substantially duplicative and should be merged into a single clause to avoid redundant drafting in the settlement clause structure.
The notice-pay clause does not clearly establish BCEA sections 37 and 38 as complementary (period-setting versus payment-mechanism) rather than as loosely related references.

The phrase implicating the manager's 'own conduct... directly implicated in the matter' should be tightened so it does not risk being read as asserting the manager formally brought or laid the charge, a fact not confirmed in the brief.
risks_to_monitor: If the Code of Practice citation defect is not corrected, the letter could be read by a sophisticated respondent or its legal representative as citing or alluding to a repealed legal instrument, undermining the letter's credibility on legal accuracy.
The duplicated compensation clauses may cause confusion for the client or the recipient as to whether two separate payments are being proposed, risking a misreading of the settlement ask.

The CCMA referral window has only 11 days remaining per the brief; the seven-day response window is appropriate but the caseworker should confirm the referral will still be timeously lodged if settlement negotiation extends past the response deadline.

The characterisation of the chairing manager's involvement, if read as alleging he laid the charge, could expose the firm to a factual overreach challenge from the employer's attorneys if that fact proves incorrect.
forensic_questions: Liability: Can the client confirm or can Northstar's records confirm who formally initiated or laid the disciplinary charge against him, as distinct from who chaired the hearing?

Liability: Did the client raise his safety concern about the brakes in writing or verbally, and is there any contemporaneous record (text message, email, incident report) corroborating the request for written instruction?
Chronology: Is the precise time the disciplinary notice was served on the client (08:00) documented anywhere, such as a text message or the notice itself?
Chronology: Was there any prior maintenance or vehicle inspection record indicating the brakes were or were not faulty, which could corroborate or undermine the safety justification?
Documents: Does the client have a copy of the disciplinary notice, the hearing minutes or outcome letter, and any applicable disciplinary code referenced at the hearing?
Documents: Has a CCMA referral (LRA Form 7.11) already been lodged or prepared, and what is the exact date of dismissal for calculating the remaining 30-day window with precision?

criteria.problem: The settlement terms include an expungement/clean-record clause referring to a 'disciplinary finding' despite the dismissal already having occurred (the finding led to dismissal, not a surviving disciplinary record to expunge in the ordinary sense); more significantly, the reference section 37/38 notice-pay clause reads as internally correct but the draft does not flag the brief's silence on prior warnings or remuneration figures, and nowhere invents a rand figure, which is good. However the agreed reference term adds an unbriefed condition ('which does not refer to the disciplinary allegation') not instructed by the client, and the non-disparagement/confidentiality terms are standard but go beyond what is confirmed as authorised terms in the brief without being flagged as such in supervisory notes.
criteria.required_fix: Confirm with the Client/caseworker whether expungement and reference-content conditions are authorised terms before including them as settlement clauses, or flag them as standard-form proposals pending instruction.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: "Confirmation that the disciplinary finding and any related record of the allegation of insubordination will be expunged from our client's personnel file" and "Provision of an agreed reference ... which does not refer to the disciplinary allegation or the circumstances of termination."

criteria.problem: The draft correctly anchors the analysis in section 188(1) before invoking the Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025, and connects the three confirmed procedural defects (short notice, no representation, biased chair) and the safety context to both liability and settlement leverage. However the compensation clause is generic: it states settlement should be calibrated 'toward the higher end' of the s194(1) range without quantifying or clearly tying the uplift to the specific HIGH-merit scoring breakdown (procedural score 9/10, substantive 7/10) in a way that reads as a reasoned escalation rather than an assertion. The HIGH merit band is not explicitly reflected in a confident but proportionate framing of litigation risk.
criteria.required_fix: Expand the exposure/settlement paragraph to explicitly tie the calibration to the three procedural defects and the safety-related substantive dispute identified in the scoring breakdown, making the reasoning for a higher-end proposal legally and factually explicit rather than conclusory.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: "our client's position is that settlement should be calibrated toward the higher end of the compensation range available under section 194(1) of the LRA, being up to twelve months' remuneration"

criteria.problem: Tone is generally professional, controlled and proportionate, consistent with the counterparty-facing profile. No emotive language, no overstated certainty. Minor stylistic issues: use of 'Most significantly' edges toward advocacy emphasis rather than restrained formulation, and the phrase 'real risk of a finding of procedural unfairness' is acceptable but borders on a qualifying hedge used inconsistently with the firm, confident register expected for a HIGH-merit case.
criteria.required_fix: Replace emphasis-adverb framing with more measured formulations consistent with house style register (e.g. 'It is material to record that the hearing was chaired by...').
criteria.evidence_from_draft: "Most significantly, the hearing was chaired by the same manager..."; "expose the dismissal to a real risk of a finding of procedural unfairness"

criteria.problem: The settlement terms list contains a clear duplication defect: the first two settlement clauses both address ex gratia/compensation under section 194(1) in near-identical terms, which is duplicated template content contrary to the required distinct, non-repetitive clause structure.
criteria.required_fix: Merge the two compensation clauses into a single settlement sub-paragraph per the standing 3A.10 order, removing the duplicate ex gratia clause.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: "Compensation on an ex gratia, total cost to company basis... settlement should be calibrated toward the higher end..." immediately followed by "Payment of an ex gratia settlement amount on a total cost to company basis, calibrated to reflect the identified procedural defects..."

criteria.problem: The response window is correctly set at seven calendar days, within the permitted maximum, and the settlement terms otherwise follow the standing 3A.10 order (notice, leave, pension, UIF, certificate of service, reference, non-disparagement, confidentiality, expungement, agreement to follow). The duplicate compensation clause reduces practical clarity and could confuse the recipient as to whether two separate payments are proposed.
criteria.required_fix: Consolidate the compensation clauses into one clear clause stating the settlement is calibrated with reference to procedural and substantive factors, expressed once.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: "We invite a substantive response to this letter within seven calendar days of receipt"; duplicate compensation clauses as above

criteria.problem: No case-law citations, no Schedule 8 reference, no rand figures, correct section 37/38 treatment as complementary ('subject to any more favourable contractual notice entitlement, with payment made in accordance with section 38 of the BCEA' reads as complementary rather than alternative), non-disparagement is correctly one-way against the employer, and the Code is correctly cited as 'Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025' at first reference. No unsupported claim that the manager 'laid' or 'initiated' a charge beyond what is confirmed (manager issued the instruction and chaired the hearing, consistent with brief). Minor: the notice-pay clause phrasing is slightly ambiguous as it reads s37 and s38 almost as sequential alternatives rather than clearly explaining s38 as the payment mechanism for the s37-derived period.
criteria.required_fix: Clarify the notice-pay clause to state explicitly that section 37 fixes the notice period and section 38 provides for payment in lieu of that notice, removing any ambiguity that the two sections operate as alternative or independent bases.
criteria.evidence_from_draft: "Payment in lieu of notice calculated by reference to the applicable notice period under section 37 of the BCEA, subject to any more favourable contractual notice entitlement, with payment made in accordance with section 38 of the BCEA"

what_is_strong: Correct and current citation of the Code of Practice: Dismissal, 2025 at first reference, avoiding the repealed Schedule 8 trap.
Section 188(1) is correctly anchored before the Code and factual reasoning is applied, satisfying the mandatory sequencing check.

The three confirmed procedural defects (short notice, denial of representation, biased chairperson) are each particularised with dates and direct quotation of the chair's conflict of interest, matching the scoring breakdown precisely.
The safety context is woven into the substantive fairness analysis without overstating certainty, using 'he says' and 'our client's account' appropriately for contested facts.

Settlement clause order substantially follows the standing 3A.10 sequence (compensation, notice, leave, pension/provident, UIF, certificate of service, reference, non-disparagement, confidentiality, record/expungement, agreement to follow).
No case-law citations, no rand figures, and non-disparagement is correctly one-way against the employer only.
what_needs_work: Duplicate ex gratia/compensation settlement clauses must be merged into a single clause consistent with the 3A.10 standing order, which permits only one compensation clause.
